title: A two-target CAR T cell, immune drugs before liver surgery, a sperm count debate
dek: A first-in-human myeloma CAR T trial in The Lancet, two immune drugs given before liver cancer surgery, a breast radiotherapy trial that narrowly misses its statistical target, and a pig model of pancreatic cancer.

tldr.text: A CAR T cell built from a natural ligand targets two myeloma proteins at once. In 15 treated patients, no dose-limiting toxicity was seen.
Giving nivolumab plus ipilimumab before liver cancer surgery was feasible in 33 patients. Tumour DNA in blood after surgery tracked who relapsed.
Genome sequencing found a likely genetic cause in 15.3 percent of 118 families with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss.
Ultrasound that briefly dampened the human hippocampus disrupted inference about how things relate (20 people).
In a small psilocybin trial for treatment-resistant depression, the main anhedonia result at week 1 was not significant.

top.title: A CAR T cell that targets BCMA and TACI shows a safe first-in-human profile in myeloma
top.gist: In 15 people with relapsed multiple myeloma, one CAR T cell aimed at two proteins caused no dose-limiting toxicity. Nine had already had BCMA-directed CAR T therapy.

evidence.limitation: Phase 1, one hospital, no control arm. The abstract reports safety; response rates were not in the text read.

top.why: Myeloma often relapses when cells lose BCMA, the usual CAR target. A CAR that also hits TACI could close that escape route, so the early safety data matter.
details: TriPRIL uses a trimeric form of APRIL, a natural protein that binds both BCMA and TACI, in place of an antibody fragment. Patients got lymphodepleting chemotherapy, then 1.0 or 3.0 x 10^8 CAR T cells. The recommended phase 2 dose was 3.0 x 10^8 cells.

Neutropenia occurred in 14 of 15 patients. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 13 of 15 (87 percent), all grade 1 or 2. One patient had grade 2 neurotoxicity and one had grade 2 haemophagocytic-like syndrome; both resolved with corticosteroids. There were no treatment-related deaths.
top.didNotShow: Not shown in the text read: how many patients responded, how long responses lasted, or that targeting TACI prevents relapse.

terms.def: A patient's own T cell, engineered to carry a receptor that finds and kills cancer cells.
A protein on the surface of myeloma cells that is the most common CAR T target in this disease.
A second surface protein on myeloma cells that binds the same natural ligand as BCMA.
A molecule that binds a specific receptor on a cell.
A fever and inflammation reaction caused by immune cells releasing signalling proteins after CAR T infusion.

diagram.caption: One engineered APRIL protein on the CAR lets a single T cell recognise two myeloma proteins.

top.forYou: Relevant to multi-antigen targeting and engineered ligand binders as a way to limit escape.

top.title: Two immune drugs before liver cancer surgery were feasible, and blood tumour DNA tracked relapse
top.gist: In 33 people with resectable liver cancer, nivolumab plus ipilimumab before surgery delayed surgery in only 2. No tumour DNA in blood after surgery went with fewer relapses.

evidence.limitation: Single-arm phase 1b with no control group. The ctDNA groups are very small (11 and 7 patients).
evidence.conflicts: Funded in part by Bristol Myers Squibb, which makes nivolumab and ipilimumab.

top.why: Giving immune therapy before surgery could lower relapse in liver cancer, but this trial only tested safety. The ctDNA signal gives later trials a candidate marker to test.
details: Patients got two doses of nivolumab and one of ipilimumab before liver resection. Three patients (9 percent) had grade 3 treatment-related events, and there were no grade 4 or 5 events. Eight patients (25 percent) had an objective response by RECIST (one complete, seven partial), and 31 (97 percent) had disease control.
Two-year recurrence-free survival was 82 percent (9 of 11) when no ctDNA was found after surgery, against 29 percent (2 of 7) when it was (p=0.049).
top.didNotShow: It did not test whether the pre-surgery drugs improve survival. That needs a randomised trial.

terms.def: Treatment given before the main treatment, here before surgery.
Fragments of tumour DNA that circulate in the blood and can be measured with a blood test.
A standard set of rules for measuring whether tumours shrink on scans.
A trial in which every participant gets the same treatment, with no comparison group.

diagram.caption: Share of patients free of recurrence at two years, by ctDNA status after surgery.

top.forYou: Relevant to combining checkpoint drugs with surgery and to ctDNA as a response marker.

top.title: Partial-breast radiotherapy missed formal noninferiority in a 3,309-patient trial, with very low recurrence
top.gist: In 3,309 women with low-risk breast cancer, 5-year recurrence in the same breast was 1.0 percent after partial-breast and 0.8 percent after whole-breast radiotherapy.

evidence.limitation: Not masked. The upper confidence limit crossed the noninferiority margin, so equivalence was not formally shown.

top.why: The absolute gap was under 0.2 percentage points, but the trial could not rule out a worse result for the shorter treatment. Readers must weigh both.
details: The IRMA trial ran in 35 centres from 2007 to 2019. Patients were aged 49 or older with tumours up to 3 cm and clear margins. The partial-breast arm got 38.5 Gy in 10 fractions twice daily. Median follow-up was 97.5 months.

The hazard ratio for recurrence with partial versus whole-breast treatment was 1.18 (90 percent CI 0.63 to 2.20). The upper limit lies above the preset margin of 1.5, which is why noninferiority was not formally shown.
top.didNotShow: It did not show equivalence, and the 5-year window says nothing about later recurrence or side effects such as cosmetic outcome.

terms.def: A trial goal: showing a new treatment is not worse than the standard by more than a set margin.
A measure of how much more or less often an event happens in one group than in another over time.
One of the separate radiotherapy doses that together make up a full course.

diagram.caption: Cumulative recurrence in the treated breast at five years in the IRMA trial.

sources.label: Journal of Clinical Oncology: IRMA trial

top.forYou: Relevant to how trials handle noninferiority margins and de-escalating radiotherapy.

top.title: Two prefrontal cell circuits separate the sensory and the emotional side of nerve pain in mice
top.gist: Imaging the mouse prelimbic cortex after nerve injury showed all inhibitory neuron classes became sensitised. Two distinct circuits drove the sensory and affective parts of pain.

evidence.limitation: Mouse work read from the abstract only. Cell counts and effect sizes were not in the text read.

top.why: Chronic pain patients often show a quiet prefrontal cortex. A circuit map that splits pain sensation from pain distress could point to more specific targets.
details: The authors used longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the same animals over time. They found that Prox1-positive interneurons from the caudal ganglionic eminence have a role, and that PV and Rbp4 neurons control the sensory dimension while Prox1 and Cux2 or Ntsr1 neurons control the affective one.
top.didNotShow: It did not test any treatment, and mouse prefrontal circuits may not map directly onto human pain.

terms.def: A part of the mouse prefrontal cortex involved in decisions, emotion and avoiding harm.
A neuron that mostly connects other neurons and often damps their activity.
Pain caused by damage to nerves themselves rather than to other tissue.

top.forYou: Relevant to cortical inhibition circuits and cancer-related neuropathic pain models.

top.title: Psilocybin did not clearly lift anhedonia at week 1 in a 20-person depression trial
top.gist: In 20 people with treatment-resistant depression, 25 mg psilocybin missed its main anhedonia endpoint at week 1 (p=0.073). Some secondary scores favoured it at week 8.

evidence.limitation: A pilot with 20 people. The primary endpoint was not significant, and the secondary results were not corrected for multiple tests.

top.why: Anhedonia, the loss of pleasure, is hard to treat. This small trial shows how mixed early psychedelic results can be, so larger trials are needed.
details: The double-blind trial gave 25 mg or 1 mg psilocybin with psychological support. The week 1 gap on the Dimensional Anhedonia Rating Scale was 11.2 points (95 percent CI -1.0 to 23.3). At week 8 it was 14.7 (2.5 to 26.8, p=0.018) and depression scores favoured 25 mg at both weeks.
top.didNotShow: It did not prove a benefit for anhedonia. The pre-set primary result was not significant.

terms.def: A loss of interest or of the ability to feel pleasure, common in depression.
Depression that has not improved after at least two standard treatments.
The one outcome a trial is designed and powered to test first.

sources.label: Journal of Affective Disorders: Novick et al.

top.forYou: Relevant to reading pilot trials where primary and secondary outcomes disagree.

top.title: Genome sequencing found a likely cause in 18 of 118 families with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss
top.gist: Sequencing 118 families whose lost pregnancies had normal chromosomes found pathogenic variants in 15.3 percent, across 17 genes. Another 10.2 percent had variants of uncertain meaning.

evidence.limitation: Descriptive study with no control group. Candidate genes still need functional proof.

top.why: About 5 percent of couples have recurrent pregnancy loss, and many get no answer. Single-gene causes could support wider testing and clearer advice on recurrence.
details: Variants lay in genes linked to disorders that are lethal around birth, such as DHCR7, PIEZO1 and SMN1. Of 28 genes with plausible variants, 15 were new candidates. Variants were inherited in 80 percent of families.
top.didNotShow: It did not show that these variants caused each loss, nor how often they recur in later pregnancies.

terms.def: Having the normal number of chromosomes.
A change in DNA that is known to cause disease.
A DNA change whose effect on health is not yet known.

top.forYou: Relevant to genome sequencing for small cohorts with rare causes.

top.title: Sellas says its AML vaccine galinpepimut-S won a phase 3 trial
top.gist: The company reports its cancer vaccine succeeded in a phase 3 trial in certain acute myeloid leukaemia patients, and a trade report says it reduced the risk of death.

evidence.limitation: Company announcement relayed by trade press. The full data were not read.

top.why: A positive phase 3 vaccine trial in AML would matter, but the numbers, the patient group and the safety data are not yet public.
top.didNotShow: Not confirmed here: the hazard ratio, number of patients, the exact population or any peer-reviewed data.

terms.def: Acute myeloid leukaemia, a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow.

top.forYou: Relevant to cancer vaccines and company-reported phase 3 endpoints.

bench.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
bench.headline: Briefly dampening the hippocampus with ultrasound made people worse at inferring new relationships from old knowledge.
bench.authors: Pan D, D'Ambrogio S, Kingston N, et al.

evidence.limitation: Small samples. Read from the abstract only, so the control condition was not checked.

bench.question: Does the human hippocampus actually cause people to use known relationships to infer new ones, or does it only light up alongside that skill?
bench.approach: People learned relational structures in a task. Imaging found structure codes in the hippocampus. A neural network predicted what disrupting those codes would do, and ultrasound tested the prediction.
bench.model: Healthy human volunteers: 36 in the behaviour and fMRI study, 20 in the transcranial ultrasound experiment.
bench.result: Ultrasound stimulation of the hippocampus disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95 percent CI -1.41 to -0.36), as the model predicted.
bench.limitations: Small groups, a lab task, and a transient effect. The abstract does not describe the control stimulation.
bench.meaning: A causal test using a non-invasive brain tool could be reused to test other brain areas and functions.

terms.def: A seahorse-shaped brain region needed for forming memories and mapping relationships.
A method that sends focused sound waves through the skull to change activity in a chosen brain area.
A measure of effect size: the size of a difference in units of standard deviation.

sources.label: Nature Human Behaviour: Pan et al.

bench.forYou: Relevant to focused ultrasound as a causal tool in the brain.

bench.title: A genetically engineered porcine model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma captures the biological complexity of the human disease
bench.headline: Pigs engineered with KRAS and TP53 changes develop pancreatic tumours that resemble the human disease, as a large-animal option beyond mice.
bench.authors: Flisikowska T, Beltran Sanguesa L, Kalla D, et al.

evidence.limitation: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Read from the abstract only, so animal numbers were not checked.

bench.question: Can a large animal that is closer to humans in size and anatomy reproduce how pancreatic cancer starts and spreads?
bench.approach: The team switched on mutant KRAS alone (KC) or with mutant TP53 (KPC) in the pancreas of midipigs. They examined tissue, ran single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry, and made pig cell lines for drug tests.
bench.model: Midipigs with KRAS G12D alone (KC) or KRAS G12D plus TP53 R167H (KPC).
bench.result: KC pigs mostly had early duct-like changes. KPC pigs progressed faster to invasive cancer with nerve invasion and early lymph spread. Cell lines responded to gemcitabine and paclitaxel like human lines, with strong sensitivity to the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3.
bench.limitations: The drug screen was exploratory, and animal numbers and survival were not in the abstract. A pig model is costly and slow.
bench.meaning: A pig model with human-like stroma and immune cells could test delivery and imaging methods that mice cannot, such as devices and nanoparticles at larger scale.

terms.def: A model carrying mutant KRAS and mutant TP53 genes that drives pancreatic cancer.
The dense scaffold of connective tissue and cells around a tumour.
A microscopic lesion in pancreatic ducts that can progress to cancer.

bench.forYou: Relevant to a large-animal PDAC model for nanoparticle penetration of dense stroma.

bench.title: Clustering of Maternal and Perinatal Complications Following Fresh and Frozen Embryo Transfer in First-Time Mothers: A Population-Based Cohort Study
bench.headline: Three of four first-time mothers had no complications after IVF, against four of five after natural conception. Multiple complications were uncommon.
bench.authors: Landsverk E, Opdahl S, Bergh C, et al.

evidence.limitation: Observational, so differences may reflect the people who need IVF rather than the treatment. Singleton first births only.

bench.question: How often do IVF pregnancies have no complications, one, or several, compared with natural conception?
bench.approach: A registry cohort across Denmark, Norway and Sweden compared deliveries after frozen embryo transfer, fresh transfer and natural conception, counting complications such as preterm birth and stillbirth.
bench.model: Registry data on singleton first-time mothers in Denmark (2008 to 2014), Norway and Sweden (2008 to 2015).
bench.result: About 3 in 4 pregnancies after either transfer type had no complications, against 4 in 5 after natural conception. Two or more complications affected 1 in 11 after IVF versus 1 in 16 naturally.
bench.limitations: Registry data cannot account for every difference in the women. Fewer frozen transfers than fresh in the cohort.
bench.meaning: Absolute gaps were small, which gives clinicians a realistic way to counsel people considering assisted reproduction.

terms.def: An IVF step in which a previously frozen embryo is thawed and placed in the uterus.
A study that follows everyone in a defined region, often using national registries.

bench.forYou: Relevant to registry designs that compare rare outcomes across countries.

bench.title: Quicklime Slaking-Mediated Exothermic Reactions in Polidocanol-Integrated Ablators with Inhibited Heat Diffusion Enable Cancer Thermal Ablation
bench.headline: Nanoparticles that make their own heat from a chemical reaction destroyed tumours in animal models, without an external heat source.
bench.authors: Zhang W, Lv Z, Peng Q, et al.

evidence.model: Liver and pancreatic tumour models (species not stated)
evidence.limitation: Preclinical, read from the abstract only. Temperatures, tumour sizes and animal numbers were not in the text read.

bench.question: Can heat for tumour ablation be made inside the tumour, rather than delivered by a laser or microwave probe that loses heat to surrounding tissue?
bench.approach: Calcium oxide (quicklime) nanoparticles with silver nanoparticles sit in a liposome shell that slows their reaction with water, which releases heat and calcium. A foam sclerosing agent, polidocanol, traps the heat and blocks tumour blood vessels.
bench.model: Subcutaneous and orthotopic hepatocellular carcinoma and orthotopic pancreatic cancer in animals.
bench.result: The authors report the ablators beat scale-matched microwave ablation and laboratory photothermal ablation in all three models. Calcium overload plus silver also produced reactive oxygen species.
bench.limitations: Only the abstract was read, so there are no numbers to quote. Safety to healthy tissue and injection route are open questions.
bench.meaning: Heat made by chemistry in the tumour could suit tumours that are hard to reach with light, such as deep pancreatic lesions.

terms.def: Killing tumour tissue by heating it.
A tiny fat-based sphere used to carry a drug or particle.
Placed in the organ where the cancer would normally arise, rather than under the skin.
Chemically reactive oxygen molecules that damage cells.

bench.forYou: Relevant to nanoparticle heat generation versus phototherapy, and to pancreatic tumour ablation.

method.title: Growing human bone marrow organoids from iPSCs
method.gist: A Bio-protocol paper describes growing 3D bone marrow organoids that make blood cells, for modelling blood disease and testing drugs on small patient samples.
method.useWhen: You want a human marrow-like niche to study blood cancers or marrow failure and test drugs, and you have iPSC culture in place.

steps.title: Make embryoid bodies
steps.text: Dissociate iPSC colonies with ReLeSR, strain through 100 um, and plate in ultra-low-attachment wells with ROCK inhibitor. About 0.12 x 10^6 cells per well; culture 24 h (day 0).

steps.title: Check size
steps.text: After 24 h the embryoid bodies should be about 100 um across.

steps.title: Induce mesoderm under hypoxia
steps.text: Switch to mesoderm and angiogenic induction medium. Culture 72 h at 1 percent oxygen. They should reach about 200 um.

steps.title: Induce hemogenic endothelium
steps.text: Swap to hemogenic endothelial induction medium and culture 48 h in normal oxygen.

steps.title: Embed in hydrogel
steps.text: Pick spheroids of about 300 to 400 um and discard fused ones. Put 20 per well of a 12-well plate on a 300 uL hydrogel base layer, and cover with another 300 uL.

steps.title: Feed and grow
steps.text: Add 1 mL of culture medium A, wait 48 h, then add another 1 mL. Organoids should sprout vessels and reach about 700 um.

pitfalls: Do not pipette the iPSC suspension up and down at plating; invert the tube two to three times instead.
Remove fused or irregular organoids before embedding.
method.safety: Follow your institution's rules for human iPSC lines, biosafety cabinets and hypoxia incubators. Patient-derived cells and mouse xenograft work need ethics approval.

terms.def: A stem cell made by reprogramming an adult cell so it can become many cell types.
A small ball of stem cells that starts to form the early tissue layers.
Blood vessel lining cells that can turn into blood stem cells.

method.forYou: Relevant to hydrogel-embedded 3D culture and drug testing on organoids.

learn.question: What does it mean when a trial says noninferior?
learn.answer: A noninferiority trial asks whether a new treatment is not worse than the standard by more than a set margin. It succeeds only if the whole confidence interval stays below that margin.
learn.analogy: Like a speed limit with a buffer: you pass only if even your worst plausible result stays inside it.
body: Before the trial, researchers choose a margin: the largest loss they would accept for a benefit such as a shorter treatment. In IRMA the margin was a hazard ratio of 1.5.

After the trial they compute a confidence interval around the difference. If its upper limit stays below the margin, the new treatment is called noninferior. If the limit crosses the margin, the result is inconclusive, even when the observed numbers look close.
IRMA showed this. Recurrence was 1.0 versus 0.8 percent, but the upper limit of 2.20 passed the margin of 1.5, so noninferiority was not formally shown.

diagram.caption: A noninferiority verdict depends on where the upper end of the confidence interval falls against a preset margin.

terms.def: A range of values that is likely to contain the true effect, given the data.
The largest loss in effect that researchers decide in advance to accept.

trials.title: PROJECTION: ctDNA before surgery and outcome in resectable pancreatic cancer
trials.what: The registry now lists this observational cohort study as terminated, with 112 participants enrolled. The reason for stopping was not read.
trials.who: People with resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, grouped by whether ctDNA was found before surgery. The main outcome is disease-free survival.

trials.title: Ketamine for depression in Alzheimer's disease
trials.what: Compares ketamine with midazolam as an active placebo. Primary outcomes are feasibility, safety and dissociation, with suicidal thoughts also tracked.
trials.who: About 30 older adults (estimated) with late-life depression and mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's disease.

chatter.title: A former NIH neuroscience director now has 32 retractions
chatter.signal: Retraction Watch report on 17 November 2026: 32 retractions, 15 this year
chatter.gist: Eliezer Masliah, former director of neuroscience at the National Institute on Aging, has 32 retractions. A 2024 investigation flagged image problems in 132 of his papers.

chatter.title: Cognito plans an FDA submission for light and sound therapy in Alzheimer's
chatter.signal: Endpoints News report from CTAD, 17 November 2026
chatter.gist: Endpoints says the company plans to file with the FDA a therapy that flickers light and sound at a set frequency. The idea began with MIT brain wave work a decade ago. Data were not read here.

chatter.title: A Lancet Oncology comment says effective cancer drugs are priced out of reach
chatter.signal: Comment published in Lancet Oncology in November 2026
chatter.gist: The comment notes that major trial results are reported each year, yet the medicines behind them can be priced beyond what many health systems can pay. Full text was not read.

chatter.title: A Lancet comment asks if all dMMR endometrial cancer patients still need chemotherapy
chatter.signal: Comment published in The Lancet in November 2026
chatter.gist: About a quarter of advanced or recurrent endometrial cancers lack mismatch repair. Adding a PD-1 or PD-L1 drug to chemotherapy has changed first-line care. Full text was not read.

chatter.title: Antibodies against the CAR itself may limit CAR T cells in brain tumours
chatter.gist: New research reported there says an antibody attack on the engineered receptor limits how long CAR T cells last in brain tumours. Preconditioning drugs or redesigned receptors helped. Data were not read.

curiosity.title: Are sperm counts really falling? Recent studies disagree
curiosity.gist: A 2017 analysis said sperm concentration in Western men fell by more than half from 1973 to 2011. A Danish study of 8,320 young men found counts stable from 1996 to 2022.
body: A reproductive scientist writing in The Conversation sets the studies side by side. The Danish study of 8,320 young men reported stable counts, though over a third had at least one measure below WHO reference levels. Irish clinic data (over 18,000 samples) showed median concentration rising from 57 to 70 million per millilitre.
She notes limits: donors and clinic patients are not the general population, labs use different methods, and one sample can mislead because values vary over time.

evidence.limitation: An expert's summary of several studies. The primary papers were not read.

terms.def: A set of measures of sperm number, movement and shape.

note: Endpoints and STAT block automated readers, so the Sellas, Cognito and Lancet comment items rest on feed text. No job could be opened and checked, so the jobs list is empty.
